title: Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis

concept.text: Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis would manufacture a handleable solid by using position-controlled chemical operations to place reactive fragments and direct their bonding throughout a prescribed three-dimensional structure. Atomic placement, composition and local bonding would become deliberate manufacturing choices. The target goes beyond drawing patterns on a surface: it requires repeated operations that extend construction into a volume while controlling errors.

Conceptual synthesis: the defining capability is controlled construction, rather than simply obtaining an orderly crystal. A convincing process would connect its sequence of positional chemical operations to the intended internal structure, including deliberately specified local features. It need not manipulate every atom separately if controlled fragment placement and bonding can reliably produce the prescribed result. The innovation remains hypothetical at macroscopic scale.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make atomic structure throughout a manufactured solid a practical design variable. The supplied research reports surface-scale control of composition, bonding and spatial placement; extending such control through a handleable object would allow manufacturing decisions at a much finer structural level. Prescribed defects, interfaces and small mechanical structures are plausible applications, conditional on reliable construction and suitable designs.

Conditional impact synthesis: useful new materials would also require stability, suitable properties and performance under operating conditions. Precise construction alone would not guarantee strength, fatigue resistance, low friction or economical production. The analogy to programmable manufacturing has limits: chemical reactions, tool access, competing reaction pathways and material stability constrain what can be built. Mechanical self-replicating factories are a further possibility requiring extensive additional capabilities, not an automatic consequence of atomic placement.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is error-controlled, three-dimensional positional chemistry at a useful scale and rate. The supplied paper identifies reliable scanning-probe synthesis using out-of-plane bonds to build extended structures as a continuing challenge. Its stated foundation is reliable placement of reactive fragments at predetermined sites, followed by iterative chemical operations on the resulting structures. Turning those operations into sustained construction throughout a growing solid is the central missing capability in this evidence base.

The reported experiment uses prepared hydrogenated silicon surfaces, molecular tool changes and operation at 4 K, and it includes off-target outcomes. These details expose concrete demands on reaction selectivity, tool preparation and handling, and the ability to continue construction after each operation. Cryogenic operation is an operating condition of this demonstration. The evidence does not show that warmer operation is necessary for success, or that temperature is a universal obstacle to mechanosynthesis.

Engineering synthesis: scaling would require maintaining tool access to construction sites, supplying reactive fragments, preserving positional control as the object grows, and detecting, preventing or correcting defects before they compromise later steps. Throughput, tool lifetime, yield and process stability would have to support a useful manufacturing rate. These are inferred requirements for the proposed capability, not experimentally established impossibility results. The supplied evidence does not resolve whether a scalable architecture can meet them together.

current_state.text: Cowie, Deimert, Groome and colleagues’ 2026 preprint, “Atomically precise mechanosynthesis of carbon structures on hydrogenated Si(100) by inverted-mode STM,” reports donation of C₂ units from surface-deposited molecules to pre-patterned reactive sites on hydrogen-passivated Si(100). The supplied review describes operation at 4 K, repeated surface patterning and extension to structures assigned as containing four carbon atoms. These are relevant demonstrations of controlled atomic-scale chemical operations on a prepared surface; they do not demonstrate a macroscopic bulk manufacturing process.

The reported structural assignments draw on imaging, simulations and exclusion of alternative interpretations. The supplied review supports describing what the authors report, but does not independently validate those assignments. Its available material included the main article and captions; supplementary material was absent, and figure images were not supplied for inspection. Those limitations constrain independent experimental and visual verification without establishing that the reported results are false.

The retained report is a preprint, and no peer-reviewed DOI was verified in the supplied research. Its arXiv v1 masthead gives 26 May 2026, while the manuscript text bears an August 24, 2026 date; the precise version chronology remains unclear. The supplied freshness search record is empty, so it cannot establish whether later work superseded this report or comprehensively determine the field’s status as of 1 November 2026. The evidence supports a surface-scale foundation while leaving macroscopic feasibility unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: build a freestanding covalent specimen at least 1 mm in each dimension through positional chemistry, with a prescribed three-dimensional internal structure. The millimetre threshold is an author-selected benchmark for a handleable bulk object, not a documented consensus standard. The demonstration should show how controlled placement and iterative bonding created the intended volume, and distinguish that contribution from conventional crystal growth or assembly of previously fabricated components.
completion_criteria.label: Positional chemistry builds prescribed freestanding covalent volumes ≥1 mm per dimension

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification: independently quantify placement or bonding errors across representative regions of the specimen’s volume, with a stated sampling plan, measurement sensitivity and statistical confidence. Diffraction could establish average crystal structure, but would not by itself verify every intended bond or local defect. Complementary local measurements should test the deliberately prescribed features. Sampled measurements can establish demonstrated accuracy and breadth; they cannot certify every bond throughout the object or prove literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent volumetric sampling quantifies placement or bonding errors with confidence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: define acceptable error rates, yield and a useful build-rate target before the trial, then report build time, tool changes, defect detection and correction, operating conditions and failed builds. Merely reporting these quantities would not establish useful performance. Repeated builds and independent replication should test whether the result is reproducible. The demonstrated scope should identify supported materials, geometries, interfaces and limits on construction access, without extrapolating a successful specimen to arbitrary structures.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated builds and independent replication test reproducibility within stated limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” and MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” concern material performance. Mechanosynthesis might offer control over defects or interfaces relevant to those goals, but precise fabrication would not establish either strength or fatigue immunity. MEC-05, “Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms,” concerns changes in mechanical configuration or behavior; atomically precise fabrication could support particular designs, while remaining a distinct manufacturing capability.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-09, “Mechanical self-replication of a production cell from feedstock,” requires an entire production system to reproduce its necessary components and functions. MEC-06 could potentially contribute a fabrication process, but does not supply that system capability. MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” concerns generating practical mechanism designs; MEC-06 concerns making prescribed structures. MEC-10, “Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures,” overlaps in constructing three-dimensional objects, but its organizing principle is growth directed by stress rather than positional control of atomic chemistry.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” share concerns about surfaces, defects and changing interfaces. Atomically precise specimens could provide controlled experimental structures for these problems. They would not by themselves establish persistent low friction or predictive models of contacts and wear, especially as surfaces evolve during service.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-08, “Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle,” and MEC-14, “Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods,” could potentially use specially fabricated materials or small mechanical structures. Their completion depends on system performance, durability and practical cost beyond manufacturing precision. MEC-03, “Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting,” likewise concerns useful conversion performance; atomically precise construction would not itself resolve that objective.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-01, “An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow,” has no direct enabling relationship established by the supplied evidence. It concerns predictive theory, while MEC-06 concerns a manufacturing process. Across disciplines, MEC-06 sits at the intersection of mechanical engineering’s positioning, tooling and process control with surface chemistry, materials science, microscopy and atomic-scale electronics.

unresolved_issues: Whether later research or peer-reviewed publication changes the assessment is unresolved because the supplied freshness search record is empty.
The relationship between the 26 May 2026 arXiv v1 masthead and the August 24, 2026 manuscript date remains unclear.
The reported structural assignments have not been independently validated here; supplementary material and figure images were unavailable to the supplied review.
A scalable architecture for sustained construction beyond surface-bound structures, with practical throughput, tool handling and defect management, remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.
Acceptable error rates, sampling confidence, yield and useful build-rate thresholds require application-specific definition; no numerical resolutions were supplied.
The proposed 1 mm benchmark is not a documented consensus criterion, and feasibility across different materials and geometries remains open.

brief.title: Solid objects built with control over every bond
possible: People could make a solid object with a planned internal arrangement of atoms and chemical bonds, the links that hold atoms together. Precisely positioned molecular fragments would build up the object through repeated reactions.
Designers could specify where different materials meet, where deliberate irregularities sit, and how tiny mechanical structures take shape inside an object.
why: Manufacturers would gain control over structure throughout a solid at the level of individual atoms. That would make the arrangement of matter inside an object a practical design choice.

sources.who: Megan Cowie and colleagues at CBN Nano Technologies
sources.showed: They report placing pairs of carbon atoms at chosen sites on silicon and extending the structures through further carbon bonding. The work is a preprint.
sources.quote: Here, we demonstrate simultaneous spatial and chemical control over the mechanosynthetic fabrication of carbon structures.
sources.cited_for: It supports controlled fragment placement followed by further bond formation.
sources.not_established: It does not establish sustained construction throughout a handleable solid.

sources.who: Qigang Zhong and colleagues at Justus Liebig University Giessen
sources.showed: They used a microscope tip to position molecular building blocks and selectively join them on a surface, while imaging changes down to individual bonds.
sources.quote:
Additionally, other complex bonding motifs such as a carbon–iodine–carbon 
connection as well as fused carbon pentagons have been installed 
in a controlled manner.
sources.cited_for: It supports building chosen molecular structures through sequential positioning and bonding.
sources.not_established: The assemblies remain surface-bound rather than freestanding solid volumes.

sources.who: Taleana Huff, Hatem Labidi and colleagues
sources.showed: They mechanically bonded a hydrogen atom carried by a microscope tip to silicon, allowing selective edits to patterns on the surface.
sources.quote:
We report the mechanically induced formation of a silicon-hydrogen covalent bond and its application in
engineering nanoelectronic devices.
sources.cited_for: It supports forming a chosen chemical bond through controlled mechanical positioning.
sources.not_established: Selective surface editing does not establish repeated construction of a solid volume.

sources.who: Eduardo Barrera and colleagues at CBN Nano Technologies
sources.showed: They used molecules as imaging probes and chemical tools, repeatedly removing individual hydrogen atoms from a silicon probe through mechanical positioning.
sources.quote:
We demonstrate this by using a novel alkynyl-
terminated molecule to reproducibly abstract hydrogen atoms from the probe.
sources.cited_for: It supports repeatable chemical operations with controlled tool and build-site positions.
sources.not_established: Hydrogen removal does not establish extended construction or useful manufacturing rates.

shown: Cowie and colleagues report placing carbon fragments at chosen silicon sites and extending them into structures assigned as containing four carbon atoms. This preprint demonstrates surface-scale operations; a handleable solid with a prescribed interior remains hypothetical.
missing: Sustained construction must extend into a growing solid while keeping reaction sites accessible and fragments precisely positioned.
A process must detect, prevent or correct errors before they disrupt later construction.
Tool handling, lifetime and fragment supply must support reliable production at a useful rate.

milestones.label: A freestanding solid with a prescribed interior
milestones.explanation: Positional chemical operations would have to build a freestanding, chemically bonded specimen at least 1 mm along each dimension, with a prescribed interior. This would establish construction throughout a handleable volume.

milestones.label: Independent measurements quantify errors throughout the volume
milestones.explanation: Independent sampling would have to measure placement or bonding errors across representative internal regions, with stated sensitivity and confidence. This would test accuracy, including deliberately specified local features.

milestones.label: Repeated builds and independent replication establish reproducibility
milestones.explanation: Repeated builds and independent replication would have to meet predefined error, yield and useful build-rate targets within stated operating limits. This would establish reproducibility and the practical scope of construction.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether a scalable system can combine site access, positional control, tool handling and error management.
Acceptable errors, measurement confidence and useful production rates depend on the intended application.
The millimetre benchmark is a proposed test, not a consensus standard; feasibility across materials and shapes remains open.

page.title: Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis
page.definition: A manufacturing process would make macroscopic solids with prescribed three-dimensional atomic composition and bonding by positioning reactive fragments to direct chemical reactions. Mechanosynthesis uses mechanical positioning to control bond formation or breaking.

goal.need: Cowie and colleagues report structures assigned as four-carbon chains, fabricated at 4 K on hydrogenated silicon. Extending such operations into a prescribed solid requires controlling errors across many interacting parts. The National Research Council identifies increasing critical-error probability with system complexity as a limitation of bottom-up manufacturing.

statements.quote: The long-term vision of all nanotechnologists has been the fabrication of a wider range of materials and products with atomic precision.
statements.context: The roadmap states that its authors’ views do not necessarily represent their affiliated organisations.

statements.quote: molecular manufacturing, defined as the construction of atomically-precise products through the use of molecular machine systems.
statements.context: The institute identifies this goal in the eligibility descriptions for its annual Feynman Theory and Experiment prizes.

statements.quote: Control beyond the surface plane is essential to building many realistic devices.

completion.title: A nanofactory makes atomically precise macroscale diamondoid products at about 0.01 kg/hour.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate the Phase XI second-generation nanofactory: manufacture atomically precise diamondoid macroscale products at approximately 0.01 kg/hour, with capacity for products up to approximately 10,000 cm³ within a 40 cm × 25 cm × 10 cm envelope.
completion.set_by: Institute for Molecular Manufacturing, Freitas–Merkle proposed research protocol, Report 58, Phase XI; written in 2008 and published in 2025.
completion.threshold_quote: manufacturing atomically precise diamondoid macroscale product objects up to ~10,000 cm3 in volume at ~0.01 kg/hour production rates.
completion.basis: This developer-set benchmark connects mechanosynthesis and hierarchical assembly to macroscopic products. It specifies one diamondoid development route, rather than a field-wide definition of completion. The report is a research proposal, not an experimental result.

milestones.title: A mechanically positioned tool donates a hydrogen atom to a selected surface site.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate hydrogen donation through mechanical forces, without electric-field-driven bond formation. The Nanofactory Collaboration prefers a diamond surface but does not require it for this benchmark. Huff and colleagues demonstrate transfer of one tip-borne hydrogen atom to a silicon dangling bond at 0 V, forming a silicon–hydrogen covalent bond.
milestones.set_by: Nanofactory Collaboration, proposed experimental benchmarks, Remaining Technical Challenges, version 1.3, section I.B.5(b).

milestones.title: A workpiece undergoes at least two successive mechanosynthetic reactions near the same reactive site.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate at least two purely mechanosynthetic diamond-mechanosynthesis reactions on or near the same reactive site of one workpiece. Cowie and colleagues report successive carbon-fragment donation on silicon, a surface-bound analogue. Barrera and colleagues report single-hydrogen abstraction in 27 of 28 trials; that single-operation result does not establish the sequence benchmark. Both reports are preprints, not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Nanofactory Collaboration, proposed diamond-mechanosynthesis experimental benchmarks, Remaining Technical Challenges, version 1.3, section I.B.5(d).
milestones.threshold_quote: a purely mechanosynthetic sequence of two or more DMS reactions

milestones.title: Mechanosynthesis produces a three-dimensional diamondoid nanostructure.
milestones.criterion: Fabricate a three-dimensional diamondoid nanostructure through purely mechanical synthesis. Diamondoid here denotes a structure with a dense three-dimensional network of strong bonds. The benchmark calls the structure significant without defining a numerical size. Zhong and colleagues demonstrate surface-bound organic trimers using voltage-pulse-assisted manipulation and coupling; these do not establish this benchmark.
milestones.set_by: Nanofactory Collaboration, proposed diamondoid experimental benchmarks, Remaining Technical Challenges, version 1.3, section I.B.5(f).
milestones.threshold_quote: purely mechanosynthetic fabrication of a significant 3D diamondoid nanostructure.

milestones.title: A nanofactory produces micrometre-scale diamondoid objects at about 0.01 kg/hour.
milestones.criterion: Operate the Phase X first-generation nanofactory with continuous bulk feedstock, mass-producing atomically precise micrometre-scale diamondoid objects at approximately 0.01 kg/hour.
milestones.set_by: Institute for Molecular Manufacturing, proposed research protocol, Report 58, Phase X.
milestones.threshold_quote: product objects at ~0.01 kg/hour production rates.

not_found: No field-wide acceptance standard specifying macroscopic size, allowable bonding-error rate and volumetric verification was found.
No published experiment meeting the IMM Phase X or Phase XI production targets was found.
No peer-reviewed journal version of the Cowie or Barrera preprint was found.

results.finding: Successive carbon-fragment transfers on silicon produced two adjacent four-carbon chains; the final step succeeded in 27 of 32 trials.
results.detail: The successive donations are a surface-bound analogue, rather than diamond mechanosynthesis. The reported 27/32 yield is for the final operation starting from its required precursor, not for the complete sequence.
results.quote:
Four successive C
2
transfers generate an eight‑carbon pattern with site‑specific placement.

results.finding: Successive coupling produced a pyrene trimer of 3 building blocks; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The surface-bound assembly involved voltage-pulse-induced bond formation, rather than purely mechanosynthetic diamond reactions.
results.quote:
Here a pyrene diradical is coupled 
with the dimer, generating a TPP 2• trimer (Fig. 4d).

results.finding: Surface-bound organic trimers contained 3 building blocks; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The products were low-dimensional organic assemblies, not three-dimensional diamondoid structures, and their synthesis used voltage pulses.
results.quote:
Here a pyrene diradical is coupled 
with the dimer, generating a TPP 2• trimer (Fig. 4d).

results.finding: One tip-borne hydrogen atom bonded to a silicon dangling bond at 0 V; number of trials not reported.
results.detail: The bond formed when the tip approached the selected site without bias or tunnel current. Tip preparation used a voltage pulse.
results.quote:
By bringing the H-functionalized tip apex very close to a DB
in the absence of bias and current, a covalent bond between
the single hydrogen and silicon atoms is formed.

results.finding: Single-hydrogen abstraction from a silicon probe succeeded in 27 of 28 trials.
results.detail: The reaction was mechanically controlled at zero bias. The authors imaged the same build site with another molecule, but did not demonstrate a second reaction there.
results.quote: This outcome – removal of a single hydrogen atom at zero volts – was observed in 27 out of 28 trials, indicating that the process is well controlled and reproducible (Methods and Supplementary Section 10).

results.finding: A tip-borne hydrogen atom passivated a selected silicon dangling bond at 0 V; total number of trials not reported.
results.detail: Hydrogen transfer occurred during AFM imaging or vertical tip approach, without an applied voltage or tunneling current during hydrogenation.
results.quote:
DB passivation is achieved by transferring the H
atom that is at the apex of an H tip to the DB, reestablishing a locally defect-free H–Si surface.

results.finding: On a Si(100) workpiece, 2 successive silicon abstractions produced a dimer vacancy; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The sequence is a surface-bound silicon analogue, not two diamond-mechanosynthesis reactions.
results.quote:
However, a second silicon abstraction event at the 
same dimer site yields a static silicon dimer vacancy (‘DV’, Fig. 4A), appearing as a dark 
depression, consistent with native dimer vacancy defects (26).
